paragraph.text: J8. "I swapped red meat for chicken, which is healthier"

the swap may make sense for the eater's health, and some health guidelines suggest replacing red meat with poultry or fish. But for animals it usually makes things worse. A cow yields on average about 364 kg of meat, a pig about 96 kg and a chicken about 1.7 kg. Kilo for kilo, swapping beef for chicken involves about 214 times more animals, and swapping pork for chicken about 57 times more. The count measures individuals, not suffering, but the difference per animal would have to be huge to offset that factor. The swap that is good for health and neutral for animals is a different one: replacing meat with legumes.
J. Practicality, economy and society ·
IND
1. Formulation
"I've stopped eating red meat. Now it's just chicken and turkey breast, which is lighter and healthier. I'm already doing my part."
There is evidence that eating a lot of red and processed meat raises some health risks (see G17).
Some health guidelines suggest replacing red meat with poultry or fish.
Eating less red meat also cuts beef consumption, which has a large environmental impact.
So swapping red meat for chicken is a good, responsible choice.

P1 has support, and P2 describes recommendations that exist. P3 is true for emissions. The problem lies in the conclusion: it looks at the eater's health and at the climate, and leaves out the number of animals killed, which rises sharply with the swap.
The argument is
as a health argument. It fails as a moral justification, because the choice that looks lighter on the plate can be the heaviest for animals.

3. Answer for children

A cow gives meat for lots and lots of meals. A chicken is small and gives meat for only a few. So if someone stops eating beef and eats only chicken, they'll need many chickens to eat the same amount of meat. Each chicken is a little animal who feels. Swapping meat for beans, lentils or chickpeas doesn't need any animal at all.
4. Short answer

For your health, the swap may make sense. But for animals it usually makes things worse. A cow yields about 364 kg of meat; a chicken, about 1.7 kg. Kilo for kilo, swapping beef for chicken involves about 214 times more animals, and swapping pork for chicken about 57 times more. And broiler chickens live only about six weeks, often with serious welfare problems. If the idea is to eat more healthily, you can swap meat for beans, lentils or chickpeas without raising the number of animals killed.
"Do you know how many chickens it takes to replace the meat from one cow?"
5. Full answer
(a) Reconstruction and diagnosis
What the argument says
What's true
What's left out

The eater's health isn't the only thing at stake
Chicken is the recommended swap

(b) Where the argument breaks

text.bold: 1. Each animal yields a very different amount of meat.

paragraph.text: According to a paper by the philosopher Daniel Dorado published in
in 2026, using Faunalytics data compiled by Our World in Data, a cow yields on average about 364.4 kg of meat, a pig about 96.1 kg and a chicken about 1.7 kg.

text.bold: 2. Kilo for kilo, the swap multiplies the animals.

paragraph.text: With these figures, replacing beef with chicken involves about 214 times more animals, and replacing pork with chicken about 57 times more. The ratios assume a complete swap, but even partial swaps add up quickly. Someone who eats 1 kg of beef consumes a small fraction of a cow; 1 kg of chicken is more than half a bird.

text.bold: 3. Fish would make the count even larger.

paragraph.text: Dorado leaves fish out because sizes vary too much between species. Since most fish eaten yield far less meat than a cow or a pig, swapping red meat for fish tends to raise the number of animals even further.

text.bold: 4. The count measures individuals, not suffering.

paragraph.text: A chicken and a cow don't go through the same things, and the number of animals doesn't say how much each one suffers. But broiler chickens aren't better off: they are slaughtered at about six weeks old (see B2), and the Welfare Footprint Project, which estimates animals' pain in each production system, documents serious welfare problems in broiler chickens, many linked to fast growth.

text.bold: 5. The link between health advice and more chicken hasn't been tested.

paragraph.text: Dorado argues that messages like "cut down on red meat", without saying what to eat instead, may lead people to chicken, because "healthy" menus and products tend to feature chicken. But he himself says this causal pathway hasn't yet been studied directly. What is certain is the arithmetic: whoever makes the swap raises the number of animals.

text.bold: 6. There is a swap that is good for health and neutral for animals.

paragraph.text: Dorado suggests that instead of recommending poultry in place of red meat, health advice could use neutral wording, such as "replace meat with legumes". Beans, lentils, chickpeas and peas provide protein without choosing which animal dies.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: a chicken doesn't suffer like a cow

The most serious version says counting heads is misleading. A chicken would have a simpler mental life than a cow or a pig, and so would suffer less. If each chicken's suffering weighs much less, the swap may not be worse.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: The difference would have to be enormous.

paragraph.text: For the swap from beef to chicken not to be worse, each chicken's suffering would have to weigh about 214 times less than each cow's. There's no evidence of a difference that large, and chickens feel pain and fear (see A5).

text.bold: Living conditions weigh against the chicken.

paragraph.text: Broiler chickens live for weeks, in sheds with thousands of birds, with health problems linked to accelerated growth. That doesn't suggest a better life than a cow's.

text.bold: Under uncertainty, prudence avoids multiplying victims.

paragraph.text: As Dorado argues, anyone who can't reliably compare suffering across species has reason to avoid choices that sharply increase the number of victims.

text.bold: The choice doesn't have to be between beef and chicken.

paragraph.text: Swapping for legumes addresses the health concern without this dilemma.
(f) Back to the moral question

The swap shows a real concern for one's own health, and that is legitimate. But the moral question is a different one: who pays for the meal? When the answer is "dozens or hundreds more animals", the choice that seemed lighter becomes heavier. If the reason to change is health, there is a change that looks after health without raising the number of deaths.

11. What the argument gets right

It's true that there is evidence of risk in high intake of red and processed meat, that some health guidelines suggest replacing it with poultry or fish, and that cutting beef reduces emissions. Whoever made the swap acted out of a real concern for health.

But for animals, the swap to chicken almost always multiplies the number of deaths. The swap that serves health without exacting that price is the one to legumes. Genuinely eating less meat, without swapping it for smaller animals, is better than doing nothing, and can be a step toward veganism; but for the animals who are still killed, the harm is still terrible.
